p: Okay, so Section 1100 of the Charter provides that every head of the department shall give his or her whole time to the duties of the office and shall not engage in any other occupation, profession, or employment. How do you reconcile this position you just said with the law?
So, wanna be really clear, the hours that I spend, which is probably 5 to 10 hours a month, is on volunteer time. It is not during my, um, TLC duties.

Section 11(1)(5) of the Charter provides that any person holding any office, whether by election or appointment, who, while during their term of office, accepts any other civil office connected with the government of the city, shall be deemed to have vacated the office. So by what authority do you claim you could remain in the office if you're appointed to the Chair of the TLC?

So I will say I sought advice from the Conflicts of Interest Board related to this, and they mentioned I did not need any waiver. I believe it may fall under the

government-to-government exception, um, and my understanding is that it did— it was cleared by
How long is your term, uh, for the- the MTA Board?
So it, um, technically ended December 31st, and I'm a holdover for the city.
Okay, um, do you have any indication, Administration, whether they will find a replacement?
I have not spoken to the Mayor about this.

Okay, just- just to clarify, this current— what COIB, uh, covers Chapter 68, right. And this is- this is not the same, uh, the Chapter or the Charter that we are talking about, just to clarify that on the record.
Okay, I'm happy to come back and discuss this with you to make sure.
It is, um, just to clear, it's chapter 49.
Okay, thank you. Yeah, I'm happy to come back, um, and we can, we can further discuss.

Thank you. So in addition to distinctions I just talked about, um, back to the issue of the, you know, remaining on the board and also be, uh, representing, um, being the CEO of TLC, just because these are two different positions. Um, can you explain why that this— it won't come up as a conflict if you stay on both?

So in terms of conflict of time, you know, I- I can do the MTA work on-on my volunteer time. In terms of potential conflicts, um, in terms of subject matter and issue, um, depending on the issue, you know, I'm happy to recuse on certain matters. I will say MTA and TLC are both entities that have similar missions, the safe and efficient transportation of passengers, and there are actually a lot of points of clarify- uh, points of collaboration that would support the public good. And so I do not believe it's a conflict, and I believe that actually, um, I have a track record of championing TLC and driver issues on the board, and I believe it is actually helpful that, um, I understand public transit issues as it relates to the TLC.

Thank you so much.
Thank you for your time today.

Thank you. Uh, thank you, Chair and Members of the Committee. Uh, I'm Justin Wood, Director of Policy at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest. We are— thank you for this opportunity to comment on the nomination of Midori Valdivia to serve as the Chair. Um, for well over a decade, New York Lawyers has worked in close partnerships with the Access-A-Ride Reform Group and the Taxis for All Coalition and other disability justice organizations to reform, uh, accessibility in both the public transit and the for-hire vehicle and taxi sectors. We're happy to support Mayor Mamdani's nomination of Midori Valdivia as Chair of the TLC. In addition to her extensive background as a public transit planner, uh, Ms. Valdivia has specific experience in bringing urgently needed accessible taxis and for-hire vehicles to New York City streets. And as an MTA board member, she has consistently championed accessibility and listened thoughtfully to transit and paratransit riders with disabilities. We'll submit a detailed, uh, set of policy recomm— recommendations into the record. We're really excited to work with the Council, with the

Administration, and with the TLC on ways to promote accessibility, reduce the climate impacts of this enormous vehicle fleet, and to promote justice for drivers in this huge industry. Um, I'll just highlight a few that came up in the hearing. Um, we are excited about the future of vehicles that are simultaneously wheelchair accessible and zero emissions and we want to continue working with the Council. We're really appreciative of a Resolution from the Council in favor of state legislation that, through a modest $1 surcharge on Uber and Lyft trips, uh, would create a large substantial $250 or more million a year fund statewide to promote accessibility, on-demand paratransit, driver justice, and electrification in the industry. So, um, we'd love to continue working with you and the TLC on that. I'll also just say, you know, our studies have consistently found that while there is progress in New York City in closing the accessibility gap with Uber and Lyft, um, it's not enough. And we'd like to see the TLC and Council disaggregate some of the data on response times for wheelchair-accessible vehicles by neighborhood.

We're excited to work on that. Um, and then finally, we'd really like to see the TLC become a leader in the region and the state, because once you cross the border from New York City to surrounding counties, there simply are no accessible vehicles. Thank you.

That- that way cannot exist when high-volume for-hire services exist alongside that medallion industry. The medallion industry was created after the Depression for one purpose: to decrease the amount of vehicles that were being taxis because everybody who had a car made their car a taxi because nobody was employed.

So the, the left-leaning Mayor at that time, Fiorello LaGuardia, decided to put out the medallion. So if you wanted to be a taxi driver, you now had to buy a medallion, and the number of taxis went down dramatically from about 30,000 or 40,000 vehicles to about 11,000 vehicles. What was the purpose of that? The purpose of that was to increase drivers' income, medallion driver income, be it an owner or a driver. It wasn't— it was to eliminate the competition so that those drivers could earn a living. The high volume for-hire services deregulated the industry. Deregulated the industry. Good afternoon, uh, good afternoon, Chair Ung and members of the industry that are present. My name is Bhairavi Desai. I'm the Executive Director of the New York Taxi Workers Alliance. We are proud to support the nomination of Midori Valdivia as the next Chair of the Taxi and Limousine Commission. It is such an honor to be on this panel in particular next to a very long-time friend from Taxis

for All campaign and next to my brother Wayne. It's honestly really heartbreaking to hear the testimonies of Wayne, and, you know, and I'm really struck by what Carmen said earlier. These are long-time veteran drivers who feel they've just never seen change. And that's because for decades now, every time we take a step forward, there is an attack against us, whether it's from the millionaire corporations to the billionaire corporations to now the trillionaires of Waymo that are hunting us down, or it's from the different interests, from the city agencies to the state and the MTA. At each step, drivers are treated as if their rights are disposable. We have to make a generational change. We cannot nickel and dime this workforce into poverty, and we cannot nickel and dime them out of poverty. Today, for example, on insurance, drivers are going from paying $400 a month to some of them as much as $1,000 a month, all because American Transit is potentially facing bankruptcy because the regulators shut their eyes to these corporations. Why are drivers the one to pay these costs? We have to end the cycle of generational poverty. We have to

end the cycle of not treating the right of drivers to feed their children and to have a decent life, to not have to work 6 to 7 days a week, 12 to 14 hours a day. It is a public good in the interest of the public good to end these working conditions and truly make a generational change. Don't let this hearing be about the CEO of Empower. Make this hearing be about the dignity of the almost 200,000 men and women and their families who depend on this job for a decent and a dignified life. Thank you.

around for 30 years, access— uh, advocating for more accessibility in the taxi world and for higher services, uh, based on universal design, uh, principles. So we appreciate your questions. Uh, when we settled with the city, a lawsuit about accessibility, uh, we advocated for a dispatch system so that wheelchair users would be able to get a taxi no matter what, wherever they were. And that program worked and worked well, uh, but the TLC, uh, claiming, uh, that it costs too much, uh, ended that program last month. And we, uh, are very hopeful that the, uh, new Chair will, uh, reestablish that program. Uh, the way it works is that if you need an accessible cab, any place in New York City, you can call this phone number or use an app. Many people can't, uh, use an app, so they can

call. If you have a speech difference, if you have a dexterity difference, you can get through. So we urge the Chair to restore this program, and we urge the Council, uh, to look at ways of helping this program go back into business. Thank you very much.

Hi, I'm Jean Ryan, President of Disabled in Action, and we are a member of Taxis for All campaign, a coalition we began in 1996, 30 years ago. Um, DIA is in favor of appointing and confirming Midori Valdivia as the Chair of the TLC. the nomination of Midori Valdivia as the next Chairperson of the Taxi and Limousine Commission. Um, the Medallion Relief Program, or MRP, has been a huge success. It's lifted thousands of drivers out of the despair of the debt crisis. To date, it's provided nearly $475 million of debt relief to over 2,000 drivers. Despite this, as you just heard from Adriano, um, hundreds of drivers, um, remain in a situation where the debt crisis never ended for them. Um, and you heard directly from Adriano about how much despair this causes. Um, this is because their lenders did not want to restructure their loans directly, which is the first step of participating in the Medallion Relief relief program. Um, the Taxi Workers Alliance, um, as soon as we realized this was the case, had been working on figuring out a solution, and we actually found one. We worked with A Company Capital, a small community development financial institution alongside the TLC, um, to create a pilot program for a slightly different version of the MRP where a new lender steps

in, pays off the old lender, and restructures the loan under the terms of the MRP. And this solution works. It works really well for the small group of drivers who were able to access it. Unfortunately, uh, company capital is small. They don't have the funding to finance the remaining loans. Um, and instead of working with the Taxi Workers Alliance to set up and find the financing needed to get that final group of drivers across the finish line, instead the Taxi and Limousine Commission ended MRP prematurely. They ended it when this group of, um, about 300 drivers, 200 to 300 drivers, have not seen any relief at all from the debt crisis. They're in the same position they were in, um, you know, 5, 10 years ago, um, that other drivers have gotten relief from. Um, and it's essential that we help these drivers access the same relief that every other driver who's had access to the MRP, um, has been able to access.

Um, we ask that the TLC, uh, stand with the Taxi Workers Alliance, um, in partnership to find this financing and finish, uh, the MRP and make sure that all drivers have access to

this historic and life-saving debt relief. Thank you.

Statement of Justin Wood and Ruth Lowenkron at New York Lawyers for the Public Interest to the NYC Council Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards, and Ethics on March 12 2026 Regarding the Appointment of Midori Valdivia as Taxi and Limousine Commission Chair

Dear Chair Ung and Members of the Committee: Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the nomination of Midori Valdivia to serve as the Chair of the New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC). For well over a decade, New York Lawyers for the Public Interest (NYLPI) has advocated for the interests of transit, paratransit, taxi, and for-hire vehicle (FHV) riders with disabilities, in close partnership with the Access-A-Ride Reform Group (AARRG!) and the Taxis for All Campaign. We strongly support Mayor Mamdani’s nomination of Midori Valdivia as Chair of the Taxi and Limousine Commission. In addition to her extensive background as a public transportation planner to this role, Ms. Valdivia has specific experience in bringing urgently needed wheelchair accessible taxis and FHVs to New York City’s streets. As an MTA board member, she consistently championed accessibility, and listened thoughtfully to transit and paratransit riders with disabilities. New York City and State need taxi and limousine regulators who prioritize accessibility while ensuring equitable compensation for drivers and reducing the climate impacts of the massive vehicle fleets dispatched on our public streets by massive corporations like Uber and Lyft, which reported a combined $58 billion in revenue last year. For far too long, riders with disabilities have been left behind in New York City and State – first, by the yellow taxi industry, and in recent years by the explosive growth of large FHV corporations. Since 2018, NYLPI has performed extensive testing to evaluate whether FHV and taxi dispatch apps like Uber and Lyft provide equivalent service to disabled and nondisabled customers. While the TLC has made progress in requiring this industry to meet minimum response time requirements for wheelchair accessible vehicle (WAV) ride requests, our recent report finds that significant disparities remain, especially in outer borough locations.

Meanwhile, New York State and populous counties adjacent to New York City have left this industry essentially unregulated, meaning that Uber and Lyft do not provide any WAV service outside of the five boroughs, making travel outside of the five boroughs burdensome or impossible for many riders with disabilities. We hope to partner with the TLC, the City Council, and with the Mamdani and Hochul administrations to simultaneously address accessibility, sustainability, and just compensation for drivers. Below are some of our relevant policy priorities:

1. Design and Availability of Accessible Zero-emissions Vehicles One global automaker recently announced a new zero-emissions van that can accommodate a side-loading wheelchair ramp. We are hopeful that similar wheelchairaccessible zero-emissions vehicles (EVs) will soon be available for sale or retrofitting in the U.S. We urge the TLC to rapidly test and approve any new WAV EV models, and to engage people with disabilities directly in designing, retrofitting, and testing such models.
